question.leadin: Answer the following bonus about the colorful history of discrimination in America.
question.text: After World War II, Joseph McCarthy was a leading proponent of the idea that America was being taken over by Communism, a belief often given this two-word name.
question.clue: Mitchell Palmer predicted an uprising on May Day during the first one of these events, in which J. Edgar Hoover organized "raids" which targeted Italian immigrants and anarchists.

swap.leadin: The Iran Hostage Crisis began during the presidency of this man.
swap.text: Name this former Georgia governor who served as president immediately before Ronald Reagan.
swap.clue: This President spoke of the "moral equivalent of war," and of "a crisis of confidence" in what would later be called the "malaise" speech.

question.leadin: Some conspiracy theorists claim that a gunman involved in this event stood on a grassy knoll, either in addition to or instead of a gunman in the Texas School Book Depository.
question.text: Name this November 22nd, 1963 event in which Texas governor John Connolly was wounded.
question.answerHtml: assassination of John F. Kennedy (accept equivalents for "assassination;" accept "JFK" for "Kennedy;" prompt on "assassination of Kennedy" alone)
question.clue: Police officer J.D. Tippit was killed shortly after this event, and both James Tague and Governor Connally were also injured in it.

swap.leadin: It was a direct violation of the Boland Amendment and it resulted in the resignations of John Poindexter and Robert McFarlane.
swap.text: Identify this affair in which military weapons were sold to a certain Middle Eastern country with payments being diverted to aid certain Nicaraguan rebels in overthrowing the Sandinistas.
swap.clue: One of the main participants in this event now runs a show called War Stories on Fox News.

question.leadin: According to notes by H.R. Haldeman, this diplomat helped the Nixon campaign sabotage the Johnson administration's peace talks in Vietnam.
question.text: Name this Secretary of State who, along with Le Duc Tho (LAY duk TAO), won the Nobel Prize for negotiating the Paris Peace Accords.
question.clue: This man, who may have coordinated the assassination of Archbishop Makarios, coined the term "constructive ambiguity" to describe his policy toward China.

swap.text: As a vice-presidential candidate under Dwight Eisenhower, Nixon gave this 1952 speech defending himself against accusations of corrupt campaign funding. It was partially inspired by the "Fala" speech of FDR.
swap.clue: Its speaker relates how his wife is a "wonderful stenographer" and "doesn't own a mink coat" and was written in response to accusations of expensing $18,000 worth of campaign funds for personal uses.

question.leadin: Identify some candidates from the 1964 U.S. Presidential election.
question.text: Nicknamed "Mr. Conservative," this Republican from Texas became the primary opponent of LBJ, but that's not saying much as he lost a very lopsided election.
question.clue: He was harmed by a message which ended "We must love one another, or we must die" after zooming in on the eye of a figure who skips the number six and repeats the number nine twice in trying to count to ten.

swap.leadin: Name some notable figures from New York political history.
swap.text: This governor of New York served as vice-president under Ford led for a time the liberal branch of the Republican party, and dealt with the Attica riots during his time as governor.
swap.clue: This man's second marriage is thought to be the reason that Barry Goldwater won the Republican nomination in 1964, and he commissioned Man at the Crossroads from Diego Rivera.

question.text: Along with North and Weinberger, John Poindexter was cited as a conspirator by this commission created by Reagan to investigate Iran-Contra. It consisted of Brent Snowcraft, Edmund Muskie, and a namesake ex-senator from Texas.
question.clue: Edmund Muskie and Brent Scowcroft were other members of this executive branch panel, led by a former Texas Senator, which criticized the Reagan administration in its 1986 report on Iran-Contra.

swap.leadin: Identify these notable Speakers of the House.
swap.text: Known as "Mr. Democrat", this man was elected to the House in 1912 and served forty-eight years in that body, including a record seventeen years as House speaker.
swap.clue: This Democratic lawmaker from Texas served as speaker for seventeen years, the longest tenure in history. Name this man who served under Eisenhower, Kennedy, Truman, and Roosevelt.

question.text: While working on Bush's campaign, Noonan coined this phrase. Bush debuted this three-word phrase, which was followed by the phrase "no new taxes," during his 1988 RNC nomination acceptance speech.
question.answer: read my lips: no new taxes
question.clue: While working on Bush's campaign, Noonan coined this phrase. Bush debuted this three-word phrase, which was followed by the phrase "no new taxes," during his 1988 RNC nomination acceptance speech.

swap.leadin: This politician gained his highest post after defeating Gerald Ford in the 1976 Presidential Election.
swap.text: Name this former Georgia governor turned President. His Vice President was Minnesota Senator Walter Mondale.
swap.clue: Jerry Brown led an "anyone but" this man campaign in a presidential primary.

question.text: In this man's first nomination acceptance speech, he mentioned a "Golden Age" that would come with the eradication of "war, poverty, and tyranny." This two-time Democratic presidential candidate declared in a later speech "eggheads of the world, unite" in reference to critiques of his intellectualism.
question.clue: This divorcee reclaimed a frequent smear by proclaiming, "Eggheads of the world, unite!"

swap.leadin: In this ad, a voice intones "We must either love each other, or we must die" over footage of a nuclear explosion.
swap.text: Identify this influential attack ad that Lyndon Johnson's 1964 campaign used to target Barry Goldwater's willingness to wage nuclear war. It depicts a girl picking the petals of a flower.
swap.clue: This famous presidential campaign attack advertisement that criticized an opponent's willingness to use nuclear weapons.

question.text: This 2004 presidential candidate and general was Supreme Allied Commander in Europe at the time of the Kosovo War. His order to attack Russian troops in Pristina Airport was disobeyed when the Lieutenant at the scene insisted it would cause World War 3.
question.clue: This former U.S. General who was the Supreme Allied Commander Europe from 1997 to 2000. In the 2004 Democratic primaries, he opted to not take part in the Iowa caucus.

swap.leadin: Name some members of the Senate active around 1950.
swap.text: This Tennessee senator chaired a namesake committee on organized crime and was Adlai Stevenson's running mate in 1956.
swap.clue: He also sponsored a bill that tightened up the Clayton Antitrust Act and ended vertical mergers, along with Emmanuel Celler.

question.leadin: This man's namesake paradox builds on work by John Maynard Keynes and explains why people prefer a medical procedure with a 70% chance of success compared to a more ambiguous procedure with a 50 to 90% chance of success.
question.text: Identify this RAND employee who was exonerated of charges filed against him for violating the Espionage Act.
question.clue: In addition to their Watergate shenanigans, G. Gordon Liddy and E. Howard Hunt broke into the office of this person's psychiatrist.

swap.leadin: Name some other things about the 1968 DNC.
swap.text: The keynote address at the DNC was delivered by this politician, who closed his speech by discussing a word that can mean either hello, goodbye, or "I love you."
swap.clue: While serving in the 442nd Infantry Regiment, this man destroyed a German bunker with a grenade he pried from his mutilated right arm, which was later amputated.

question.text: John D'Agata's About a Mountain documents the proposed nuclear waste repository to be located beneath this Nevada landform.
question.clue: Underground tests produced so much nuclear waste that the government opened up a nuclear repository inside this mountain in 1982. The Nellis Air Force Range testing includes this mountain's namesake lake and flat.

swap.leadin: This term was popularized by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. FTPE.
swap.text: Identify this term, used in the title of a 1973 Schlesinger book about Richard Nixon's regime, and often applied to Andrew Jackson, Franklin Roosevelt, and other U.S. regimes characterized by an assertive use of executive power.
swap.clue: This two-word term coined by Arthur Schlesinger in a book of the same name. In it, Schlesinger argued that the title office had become too powerful.
